summary.text: A binary star is a system of two stars held together by gravity, orbiting each other around a common center of mass.
Binary stars are among the most important objects in astrophysics because they allow direct measurement of stellar masses and test theories of stellar evolution.
Close pairs can exchange mass, which may bring their evolution to stages that single stars cannot reach.

items.prompt: Two stars look close together in the sky. Why can't astronomers assume they form a binary?

options.label: They may lie along one line of sight at very different distances
Binary stars must always look far apart in the sky
Only stars of equal brightness can form a binary
Close-looking stars are always too young to orbit

items.explain: Double stars may be binaries or merely two stars that appear close in the sky but have vastly different true distances, called optical doubles.

items.prompt: In 1767 John Michell asked how likely it was that so many stars sit in pairs by chance. What did his answer suggest?

options.label: Stars are spread evenly at random across the sky
Many pairs are real systems, not chance alignments
Pairs only seem to exist because telescopes blur nearby stars
Most pairs are chance alignments of faraway stars

items.explain: He showed that more stars occur in pairs or groups than random distribution could explain, and concluded they may be drawn together by gravity.

items.prompt: Herschel hoped to use pairs of stars to measure distance. By 1803 he saw their relative positions shifting over 25 years, not as parallax would. What did he conclude?

options.label: The pairs were drifting apart as the universe grew
Earth's own orbit had changed since he started
His telescope's lens had warped over time
Stars in several pairs were circling one another

items.explain: Instead of parallax changes, the stars seemed to be orbiting each other in binary systems.

items.prompt: A star's light dips on a regular schedule. What two-star system could explain this?

options.label: A pair whose orbit is edge-on, so each passes in front of the other
A pair whose orbit is face-on, so neither passes in front
A pair too far apart to orbit one another
A pair seen only as two stars in a telescope

items.explain: A binary orbiting in a plane along our line of sight will eclipse and transit, changing brightness; these are photometric binaries.

items.prompt: A dim star sits right next to a very bright one. Why might a telescope fail to reveal the dim one?

options.label: The bright star's glare can hide the fainter one
Dim stars cannot be bound to bright ones
Binary stars can only be seen if both are equally bright
Bright stars always orbit too slowly to track

items.explain: The relative brightness of the two stars matters, as glare from a bright star may make it difficult to detect a fainter component.

items.prompt: A lone star and a very close pair begin life alike. What lets the pair reach stages the loner never will?

options.label: They share one core, so they burn fuel twice as long
Their light heats each other and keeps both burning forever
They can trade material, which changes how each one ages
Their orbit slows time, so they age faster

items.explain: Close binaries can exchange mass, which may bring their evolution to stages that single stars cannot attain.

paragraphs.heading: Two stars, one orbit
paragraphs.text: A binary star is a pair of stars held together by their gravity and circling each other. Today the name is usually kept for pairs that revolve around a shared center of mass. The looser term double star covers any two stars that simply look close together in the sky. Some doubles are true binaries, but others are optical doubles: two stars at very different distances from the Sun that only happen to line up.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Binaries are among the most important objects in astrophysics. Studying them lets astronomers measure the masses of stars directly and put theories of how stars evolve to the test. When the two stars sit close together, their gravity can pull each other's outer atmospheres out of shape. Some close pairs even trade mass, which can carry them into stages a lone star never reaches. Binaries also sit at the heart of many planetary nebulae, and they give rise to novae and type Ia supernovae.

paragraphs.heading: Four ways to spot one
paragraphs.text: Astronomers sort binaries by how they are detected. A visual binary is one that a telescope can split into two separate stars. A spectroscopic binary reveals itself through periodic changes in its spectral lines. A photometric binary dims when one star eclipses the other, and an astrometric binary shows up when a star's position strays because of a companion nobody can see. A single pair can belong to more than one of these groups.

paragraphs.heading: Mapping an orbit
paragraphs.text: In a visual binary, the brighter star is called the primary and the dimmer one the secondary. Each time they look, observers note the direction and the angular gap from the primary to the secondary, along with the time. After enough of these records, they plot the points around the primary and fit the most likely ellipse that obeys Kepler's law of areas. That shape, the apparent ellipse, is the real orbit projected onto the plane of the sky.

paragraphs.heading: Early discoveries
paragraphs.text: Pairs of stars that look close together have been seen ever since the telescope was invented; Riccioli saw Mizar in the Big Dipper as double in 1650. In 1767 John Michell used statistics to show that stars come in pairs and groups far more often than chance alignment could explain, and he suggested gravity might draw them together. William Herschel began watching double stars in 1779, hoping to use them to measure the distance to nearby stars. By 1803 he had seen many pairs shift over 25 years in a way that looked like orbiting rather than parallax.

paragraphs.heading: Famous pairs and big catalogs
paragraphs.text: Sirius is a binary, and so is Cygnus X-1, a well-known black hole. The first binary orbit ever worked out was that of Xi Ursae Majoris, computed by Félix Savary in 1827. As of June 2017 the Washington Double Star Catalog listed more than 100,000 double stars, yet orbits are known for only a few thousand. Many visual binaries need centuries or millennia to go around once, and for most of them only part of a circuit has been seen.
